Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

Clinical Vignette: Thao

Thao was sixty-two when his youngest son, Minh, drowned during a fishing expedition off the coast of North Carolina. It was a summer morning in 2019, the kind of bright, ordinary day that Thao had known for forty years at sea. Minh, then twenty-eight, had wanted to learn the family trade-had insisted on it, in fact, over his mother's protests. They were checking nets three miles offshore when the current shifted. Minh, who had never been a strong swimmer despite growing up in a fishing family, lost his footing on the slick deck. Thao saw him go over the rail. He heard the splash. He dove, but the water was dark and cold, and by the time the Coast Guard arrived, Minh had been under for nearly ten minutes. They recovered his body two days later. At the funeral, Thao sat motionless in his dark suit, feeling nothing-or rather, feeling as though something essential had been hollowed out and replaced with a weight that would never lift.

In the months after Minh's death, Thao returned to fishing. His wife, Linh, had begged him not to. But the boat was how he had always made sense of the world, and the alternative-sitting at home with his grief-felt impossible. What he did not anticipate was that the water itself had become a landscape of danger. Within weeks of going back out, he began to experience sudden, overwhelming physical reactions. The smell of salt spray would trigger a racing heart and a sensation of drowning that lasted for hours. Once, when a younger crew member slipped on deck, Thao's hands began to shake so violently he had to sit down, gripping the rail until his knuckles whitened. He was certain something terrible was about to happen again-that the sea was waiting to take someone else, perhaps him, perhaps one of the men who depended on him. His sleep deteriorated. He would lie awake beside Linh, his body rigid with tension, replaying the moment of the splash over and over, wondering if there was something he should have seen, something he could have done differently. The anger came too, sudden and hot-at Minh for being careless, at himself for allowing his son on the boat, at God for the senselessness of it all.

What made everything worse was the certainty that had settled into Thao's mind: people could not be trusted to keep themselves safe, not even-or especially not-the ones you loved most. He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing standing between his family and disaster. His wife had survived; his older son had survived. But they could be taken at any moment, and there was nothing he could do to prevent it. This belief hardened into something almost paranoid. When Linh mentioned going to the grocery store, Thao felt a spike of dread-what if something happened while she was driving? When his older son called late, Thao's first thought was that something had happened to him. These fears fed the physical reactivity that now governed his days. A car horn outside the house would send his heart into his throat. The sight of water-even the rain-filled gutter beside their driveway-could trigger that suffocating sensation of drowning, that certainty that death was close. And each time his body reacted this way, it confirmed what he now believed: the world was fundamentally unsafe, and the people around him were vulnerable in ways he could not control. He felt dead inside most of the time, as though the part of him that had died with Minh was the only part that had ever truly been alive. The guilt was relentless-he had survived, and Minh had not. Why? What had he done to deserve another day when his son would never have another?

Thao stopped going out on the boat regularly, though he could not admit this to his fishing crew. Instead, he found reasons to stay ashore-equipment repairs, administrative tasks, things that kept him from the water. His income dropped noticeably. Linh began working extra shifts at the hospital where she was a nurse, and the tension between them grew thick and silent. He withdrew from the Vietnamese community gatherings they had attended for decades, afraid of the questions, the sympathy, the inevitable conversations that would circle back to Minh. Now, at sixty-two, Thao sits in the waiting room of a therapist's office, referred by his primary care physician who had noted his blood pressure climbing steadily over the past three years. He is not sure why he agreed to come. Part of him believes that talking about what happened will only make it worse, that acknowledging the danger he feels will somehow invite it closer. But another part of him-the part that watches Linh's exhaustion, that hears the strain in his older son's voice when he calls-knows that something has to change. He is terrified that if he loosens his grip on the vigilance that has kept him alive, something catastrophic will happen. And he is equally terrified that he will feel this way forever, dead inside, unable to trust that anyone he loves will make it through another day.
